implementation_notes: Apache Camel implements the pattern as a first-class EIP: routingSlip(expression) computes the slip once from a header or expression (comma-delimited endpoint URIs by default), routes the exchange through those endpoints pipeline-style, and records progress in the Exchange.SLIP_ENDPOINT property so the current position is observable. Camel's own documentation is explicit that the slip is computed beforehand - use Dynamic Router when the next hop must be decided per hop - and it offers ignoreInvalidEndpoints and allowedSchemes as the two safety valves for untrusted slips. This is the default Java realization because Camel's EIP vocabulary is the reference implementation of the catalog.
pitfalls: The slip is computed once when the exchange enters the EIP, so a step that tries to add or reorder entries later needs Dynamic Router instead.
Endpoint URIs come from a header and therefore from the message producer: without allowedSchemes or a whitelist, a forged slip can reach arbitrary components.
Slip endpoints are resolved at runtime, so a typo or a renamed route fails the exchange mid-flow - turn on ignoreInvalidEndpoints deliberately, not by default.

variants.name: Hand-rolled UnaryOperator itinerary
variants.implementation_notes: Without an ESB, Java 8 lambdas reduce the pattern to a list of UnaryOperator<Envelope> (or Function<Message, Message>) on an immutable envelope record with a cursor, applied by a while loop; this replaces the classic Router/Step class hierarchy with function composition and makes each step a lambda that a planner can assemble per message. It is the right realization inside a single service, a Spring bean or a test, and it composes with CompletableFuture when steps are asynchronous. Keep the classic class-based structure when steps need injected collaborators - then Spring Integration's routing-slip router (documented in its Router Implementations chapter, with a slip-index header on the message) is the framework answer.
pitfalls: A slip of lambdas is not serializable, so it cannot be sent through JMS/Kafka: put step ids in the message and resolve them against a registry.
Exceptions thrown by a step abort the loop after earlier steps have committed; Java gives no automatic undo, so steps must be idempotent or paired with compensating actions.
Unbounded itineraries built with List.of(...) / stream collectors leak memory into headers when messages are large or slips are long - bound the length and validate ids.
